newsitem.title: HONG KONG: US wheat diverted from China said not TCK tainted.
newsitem.headline: US wheat diverted from China said not TCK tainted.

text.p: A consignment of U.S. wheat originally destined for China, but diverted to the Philippines, was certified free of a potentially harmful fungus before it was loaded, a trader close to the deal said on Friday.
Reports the wheat had been rejected by China because it was infected with the TCK smut fungus were untrue, he said.
"It was not rejected by China," the trader said.
"It never reached Chinese waters so it has not been inspected by the Chinese," he said on condition of anonymity.
One vessel carrying 33,800 tonnes of soft red winter wheat from the U.S. Midwest corn belt was diverted at sea because of port congestion in Shanghai, he said.

The executive director of the Philippine Association of Flour Millers Inc (PAFMIL), Ric Pinca, said he had been offered the wheat, "but I did not show any interest because we have not been using such wheat".

Nor was he able to confirm that PAFMIL members -- who account for 80 percent of all Philippine wheat imports and usually buy dark northern spring wheat and western white wheat -- had bought the grain.

Traders in the Philippines said on Thursday three local firms had bought, for a large discount, 35,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat originally destined for China priced at $192 a tonne. They said the wheat could either be used for noodles and pastries, or as animal feed.
"PAFMIL has no knowledge of any purchases by any of its members," Pinca said, adding he had asked members to report any purchases of the diverted wheat.
Up to 90 percent of the 2.3 million tonnes of wheat imported by the Philippines in 1995 came from the United States, the trading source said, and all of that from the U.S. Pacific northwest region.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) says it cannot guarantee wheat from this area as free of TCK. China does not import any U.S. wheat from the Pacific northwest because it has a policy of not accepting wheat without the guarantee.
The USDA had certified the wheat now bound for the Philippines as free of TCK, and the cargo carries an official quarantine certificate to that effect, the trader said.

Up to 12 vessels loaded with 400,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat were already moored in Shanghai, he said, clocking up huge demurrage fees for the buyer, Beijing's central food trading arm China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import Export Corp (COFCO). The company was not immediately available for comment.
Cofco buys U.S. wheat on an FOB (free on board) basis and so is responsible for demurrage charges incurred by port delays.

Trading sources have said up to 500,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat is sitting in Chinese ports waiting to be discharged while quarantine authorities test it for TCK smut and, if it is tainted, work out how to it can be treated and accepted.
TCK smut has been a simmering issue between Beijing and Washington since 1974, when China first declared its zero tolerance policy.
TCK is a parasitic fungus that can cut yields by up to 30 percent, according to an agricultural officer with Hong Kong's Agriculture and Fisheries Department.
The fungus is resistant to fungicides, cannibalises the plant and replaces the grain embryos with its own black spores, and remains present in soil for up to a decade, she said.
China is the world's biggest wheat importer and one of the biggest buyers of U.S. wheat. Imports in 1995 totalled 11.59 million tonnes, with 3.8 million tonnes from the United States.
Exporters have already shipped more than 800,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat to China this year.
Another 1.4 million tonnes of orders have been cancelled, mainly because the domestic wheat harvest is expected to be a record 107 million tonnes.
China's total wheat imports are expected to be down to eight million tonnes for this year, mostly bought from Canada.
